paper_title: Directing Energy Transport in Organic Photovoltaic Cells Using Interfacial Exciton Gates

knowledge_points.content: Exciton permeable interfaces, also known as passive exciton gates, direct exciton transport by introducing a symmetry-breaking imbalance in energy transfer rates (k12/k21) between two materials.
knowledge_points.evidence: These interfaces introduce a symmetry-breaking imbalance in exciton energy transfer, leading to directed motion... Such passive exciton gates break the symmetry associated with normal diffusion and exploit transport in an apparent superdiffusive regime.

knowledge_points.content: An energetic asymmetry for exciton gating can be realized using an energy-cascade structure where a wider energy gap donor (e.g., SubPc, Eg = 2.0 eV) transfers excitons to a narrower energy gap donor (e.g., SubNc, Eg = 1.8 eV), making reverse transfer energetically improbable.
knowledge_points.evidence: Material 1 in Figure 1a may be a donor material with a larger energy gap than Material 2... SubPc (Eg = 2.0 eV) to boron subnaphthalocyanine chloride (SubNc, Eg = 1.8 eV)... whereas the reverse transfer is very improbable with R0 ~ 0 nm.

knowledge_points.content: Exciton gating can be achieved through molecular site density asymmetry at the interface between a dilute donor layer (donor in a wide-gap matrix) and a neat donor layer, where the higher density of sites in the neat layer biases the hopping rate.
knowledge_points.evidence: Material 1 is a layer of donor material diluted into a wide energy gap matrix, while Material 2 is a neat layer of the same donor... dilution reduces the number of molecular destination sites in the dilute layer relative to the neat layer... the site imbalance creates an asymmetry in hopping rates.

knowledge_points.content: Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) simulations of exciton permeable interfaces reveal a discontinuity in steady-state exciton density, characterized by a depletion on the side where transfer is unfavored and a pile-up on the side where transfer is favored.
knowledge_points.evidence: The presence of imbalance, however, leads to a discontinuity in the exciton density at the permeable interface. The discontinuity reflects a depletion and pile-up of excitons, with a net movement toward the side of the interface to which energy transfer is favored.

knowledge_points.content: An energy-cascade OPV utilizing a 10 nm SubPc layer and a 6 nm SubNc layer paired with a C60 acceptor achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 4.4 ± 0.2%.
knowledge_points.evidence: measurements of the power conversion efficiency (ηP) reveal that these devices can be quite efficient with ηP = (4.4 ± 0.2)% when incorporating a 6 nm-thick SubNc layer.

knowledge_points.content: In dilute donor OPVs (SubPc in UGH2), the exciton diffusion efficiency (ηD) of the dilute layer increases from 56.9% to a maximum of 74.6% upon dilution, with 80% of this enhancement attributed to the gating effect at the interface rather than bulk diffusion length increases.
knowledge_points.evidence: The ηD(Dilute) increases from (56.9 ± 1.1)% to a maximum value of (74.6 ± 1.5)%. Of this enhancement, 20% results from favorable changes in bulk LD with the remainder resulting from the gating effect of the interface.

knowledge_points.content: Increasing the number of exciton permeable interfaces in a multilayer structure leads to apparent superdiffusive exciton transport, where the mean-squared displacement follows <x²> = βt^α with α reaching values as high as 1.5.
knowledge_points.evidence: Clearly, the structures with the greatest number of permeable interfaces show the largest degree of apparent superdiffusive motion, with α reaching a peak value of ~1.5.

knowledge_points.content: The Förster radius (R0) for energy transfer from the donor SubPc to the donor SubNc is calculated to be 2.1 nm, facilitating downhill energy transport in cascade devices.
knowledge_points.evidence: A prediction for the Forster radius (R0) from SubPc to SubNc yields R0 = 2.1 nm, whereas the reverse transfer is very improbable with R0 ~ 0 nm.

knowledge_points.content: Multilayer photoluminescence quenching experiments using NTCDA as a quencher confirm the presence of exciton gating, as experimental PL ratios only match simulations when the interfacial rate imbalance is included.
knowledge_points.evidence: Agreement between experimental and simulated photoluminescence ratios is only achieved when imbalance (gating) at the permeable interface is included (Figure 3b).

knowledge_points.content: By utilizing exciton gates, a total donor layer diffusion efficiency (ηD) greater than 85% can be achieved in planar heterojunction architectures without the need for bulk heterojunction (BHJ) morphologies.
knowledge_points.evidence: Remarkably, a total donor layer ηD > 85% is achieved without resorting to a corrugated interface morphology or a BHJ architecture where the large D-A interfacial area circumvents diffusion altogether.

knowledge_points.content: The OPV devices in this study were fabricated using vacuum thermal sublimation at pressures below 10^-7 Torr, with organic layers deposited at a rate of 0.2 nm/s.
knowledge_points.evidence: Organic layers were deposited via vacuum thermal sublimation (<10^-7 Torr) at a nominal rate of 0.2 nm/s.

knowledge_points.content: Exciton gates allow excitons to traverse multilayer structures on timescales shorter than their natural lifetime; for example, 20% of excitons can traverse a 16 nm structure even when the average diffusion length (LD) is only ~6 nm.
knowledge_points.evidence: Indeed, nearly 20% of excitons injected into bin 1 are able to traverse the 16 nm layer structure in the 16-layer system even though the average LD is only ~6 nm. Furthermore, these excitons are collected on a dramatically shorter time scale with the majority being transported below their natural exciton lifetime of τ = 1 ns.
